observations.limitations: The examples establish food-sauce uses but do not define the full consistency range.
observations.observation: The article names “saus keju,” “saus tomat,” “saus sambal,” and sauces served with siomay, bakso, and noodles.
observations.source_title: Kenali Anak dengan Sindroma Nefrotik dan Diet Sehatnya

observations.limitations: It supports natural generic and specific use, not a measured claim of nationwide normality; “sambal” and “kecap” also name particular condiments.
observations.observation: The article uses both generic “saus” and specific expressions such as “saus tomat” and “saus kacang.”
observations.source_title: Kenali Anak dengan Sindroma Nefrotik dan Diet Sehatnya

observations.limitations: A regulatory product list is not evidence of conversational frequency.
observations.observation: Food categories include “saus cabe,” “saus tomat,” “saus tiram,” and other named sauces, alongside “sambal.”
observations.publisher: Badan Pengawas Obat dan Makanan Republik Indonesia

observations.limitations: The page also has an unrelated uppercase SOS entry; the dictionary alone does not establish preference.
observations.observation: The food sense defines “sos” as a liquid or thick substance used to enhance food's flavour.

observations.limitations: This is a generic use in one institutional publication, not a frequency comparison.
observations.observation: Food advice says to flavour meat, fish, and chicken with lime juice, spices, “sos,” and natural seasonings.
observations.publisher: Institut Kanser Negara, Kementerian Kesihatan Malaysia
observations.source_title: Panduan Mengatasi Masalah Pemakanan Kesan Dari Rawatan Kanser

observations.limitations: This is a named product, and the database is associated with 1997; the generic contemporary use is better shown by the separate nutrition guidance.
observations.observation: The database labels bottled chilli sauce “Sos cili dalam botol.”
